claim: Subcortical structures play a critical role in speech processing by performing important functions such as localizing sound.
source: Subcortical structures play a critical role in this process – they do not merely relay information from the periphery to the cortex, but also perform important functions for speech understanding, such as localizing sound (e.g., Grothe and Pecka, 2014) and encoding vowels across different levels and in background noise (e.g., Carney et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Grothe and Pecka, 2014.

claim: Subcortical structures encode vowels across different levels and in background noise.
source: Subcortical structures play a critical role in this process – they do not merely relay information from the periphery to the cortex, but also perform important functions for speech understanding, such as localizing sound (e.g., Grothe and Pecka, 2014) and encoding vowels across different levels and in background noise (e.g., Carney et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carney et al., 2015.

claim: Subcortical structures receive descending information from the cortex through corticofugal pathways.
source: Furthermore, subcortical structures receive descending information from the cortex through corticofugal pathways (Bajo et al., 2010; Bajo and King, 2012; Winer, 2005), suggesting that they may also play an important role in modulating speech and auditory streaming.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bajo et al., 2010; Bajo and King, 2012; Winer, 2005.

claim: The auditory nerve contributes to ABR waves I and II at approximately 1.5–3 ms latency.
source: The ABR's component waves have been attributed to activity in different subcortical structures with characteristic latencies: the auditory nerve contributes to waves I and II (~1.5–3 ms), the cochlear nucleus to wave III (~4 ms), the superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus to wave IV (~5 ms), and the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to wave V (~6 ms) (Møller and Jannetta, 1983; review by Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Møller and Jannetta, 1983; Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976.

claim: The cochlear nucleus contributes to ABR wave III at approximately 4 ms latency.
source: The ABR's component waves have been attributed to activity in different subcortical structures with characteristic latencies: the auditory nerve contributes to waves I and II (~1.5–3 ms), the cochlear nucleus to wave III (~4 ms), the superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus to wave IV (~5 ms), and the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to wave V (~6 ms) (Møller and Jannetta, 1983; review by Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Møller and Jannetta, 1983; Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976.

claim: The superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus contribute to ABR wave IV at approximately 5 ms latency.
source: The ABR's component waves have been attributed to activity in different subcortical structures with characteristic latencies: the auditory nerve contributes to waves I and II (~1.5–3 ms), the cochlear nucleus to wave III (~4 ms), the superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus to wave IV (~5 ms), and the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to wave V (~6 ms) (Møller and Jannetta, 1983; review by Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Møller and Jannetta, 1983; Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976.

claim: The lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus contribute to ABR wave V at approximately 6 ms latency.
source: The ABR's component waves have been attributed to activity in different subcortical structures with characteristic latencies: the auditory nerve contributes to waves I and II (~1.5–3 ms), the cochlear nucleus to wave III (~4 ms), the superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus to wave IV (~5 ms), and the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus to wave V (~6 ms) (Møller and Jannetta, 1983; review by Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Møller and Jannetta, 1983; Moore, 1987; Starr and Hamilton, 1976.

claim: ABR waves I, III, and V are most often easily distinguished in the human response.
source: Waves I, III, and V are most often easily distinguished in the human response.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about human ABR responses.

claim: Subcortical structures may contribute to the earlier P0 (12–14 ms) and Na (15–25 ms) waves of the middle latency response.
source: Subcortical structures may also contribute to the earlier P0 (12–14 ms) and Na (15–25 ms) waves (Hashimoto, 1982; Kileny et al., 1987; Picton et al., 1974) of the middle latency response (MLR), which are then followed by thalamo-cortically generated waves Pa, Nb, and Pb/P1 (Geisler et al., 1958; Goldstein and Rodman, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hashimoto, 1982; Kileny et al., 1987; Picton et al., 1974.

claim: MLR waves Pa, Nb, and Pb/P1 are thalamo-cortically generated.
source: Subcortical structures may also contribute to the earlier P0 (12–14 ms) and Na (15–25 ms) waves (Hashimoto, 1982; Kileny et al., 1987; Picton et al., 1974) of the middle latency response (MLR), which are then followed by thalamo-cortically generated waves Pa, Nb, and Pb/P1 (Geisler et al., 1958; Goldstein and Rodman, 1967).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Geisler et al., 1958; Goldstein and Rodman, 1967.

claim: ABR and MLR waves have a low signal-to-noise ratio and require numerous stimulus repetitions to record a good response.
source: ABR and MLR waves have a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and require numerous stimulus repetitions to record a good response.
evidence: This is stated as a general characteristic of ABR and MLR recordings.

claim: A technique that extracts the fundamental waveform from speech and finds the envelope of the cross-correlation with EEG data produces a response with an average peak time of about 9 ms.
source: One such technique extracts the fundamental waveform from the speech stimulus and finds the envelope of the cross-correlation between that waveform and the recorded EEG data (Forte et al., 2017). The response has an average peak time of about 9 ms, with contributions primarily from the inferior colliculus (Saiz-Alía and Reichenbach, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forte et al., 2017 and Saiz-Alía and Reichenbach, 2020.

claim: The cross-correlation response to fundamental waveform has contributions primarily from the inferior colliculus.
source: One such technique extracts the fundamental waveform from the speech stimulus and finds the envelope of the cross-correlation between that waveform and the recorded EEG data (Forte et al., 2017). The response has an average peak time of about 9 ms, with contributions primarily from the inferior colliculus (Saiz-Alía and Reichenbach, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saiz-Alía and Reichenbach, 2020.

claim: A deconvolution technique using rectified broadband speech waveform as input and EEG as output can compute the ABR waveform as the impulse response.
source: A second technique considers the rectified broadband speech waveform as the input to a linear system and the EEG data as the output, and uses deconvolution to compute the ABR waveform as the impulse response of the system (Maddox and Lee, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maddox and Lee, 2018.

claim: The speech-derived ABR shows a wave V peak whose latency is highly correlated with the click response wave V across subjects.
source: The speech-derived ABR shows a wave V peak whose latency is highly correlated with the click response wave V across subjects, demonstrating that the component is generated in the rostral brainstem.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the deconvolution technique, implicitly referencing Maddox and Lee, 2018.

claim: Cheech stimuli interleave alternating octave frequency bands of speech and chirps aligned with some glottal pulses.
source: A third technique averages responses to each chirp (click-like transients that quickly increase in frequency) in re-synthesized 'cheech' stimuli (CHirp spEECH; Backer et al., 2019) that interleaves alternating octave frequency bands of speech and chirps aligned with some glottal pulses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Backer et al., 2019.

claim: Brainstem responses to cheech stimuli show a wave V but do not show earlier waves.
source: Brainstem responses to these stimuli also show a wave V, but do not show earlier waves (Backer et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Backer et al., 2019.

claim: Broadband peaky speech evokes canonical ABR waves I, III, and V in adults with normal hearing.
source: Figure 1 shows that waves I, III, and V of the canonical ABR are clearly visible in the group average and the individual responses to broadband peaky speech, which were filtered at a typical high-pass cutoff of 150 Hz to highlight the earlier ABR waves.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: Waves I and V were identifiable in responses from all 22 subjects to broadband peaky speech.
source: Waves I and V were identifiable in responses from all subjects (N = 22), and wave III was identifiable in 19 of the 22 subjects.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Wave III was identifiable in 19 of 22 subjects in responses to broadband peaky speech.
source: Waves I and V were identifiable in responses from all subjects (N = 22), and wave III was identifiable in 19 of the 22 subjects.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Mean peak latencies for ABR waves I, III, and V to broadband peaky speech were 3.23 ± 0.09 ms, 5.51 ± 0.07 ms, and 7.22 ± 0.07 ms, respectively.
source: Mean ± SEM peak latencies for ABR waves I, III, and V were 3.23 ± 0.09 ms, 5.51 ± 0.07 ms, and 7.22 ± 0.07 ms, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Inter-wave latencies for broadband peaky speech were 2.24 ± 0.06 ms for I–III, 1.68 ± 0.05 ms for III–V, and 4.00 ± 0.08 ms for I–V.
source: Inter-wave latencies were 2.24 ± 0.06 ms (N = 19) for I–III, 1.68 ± 0.05 ms (N = 19) for III–V, and 4.00 ± 0.08 (N = 22) for I–V.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Peak inter-wave latencies for peaky speech fall within the range expected for brainstem responses.
source: These peak inter-wave latencies fall within a range expected for brainstem responses, but the absolute peak latencies were later than those reported for a click ABR at a level of 60 dB sensation level (SL) and rate between 50 and 100 Hz (Burkard and Hecox, 1983; Chiappa et al., 1979; Don et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to cited literature (Burkard and Hecox, 1983; Chiappa et al., 1979; Don et al., 1977).

claim: Absolute peak latencies for peaky speech were later than those reported for click ABR at 60 dB SL and rate between 50 and 100 Hz.
source: These peak inter-wave latencies fall within a range expected for brainstem responses, but the absolute peak latencies were later than those reported for a click ABR at a level of 60 dB sensation level (SL) and rate between 50 and 100 Hz (Burkard and Hecox, 1983; Chiappa et al., 1979; Don et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to cited literature (Burkard and Hecox, 1983; Chiappa et al., 1979; Don et al., 1977).

claim: Broadband peaky speech evoked waves I, often III, and P0 in addition to waves V, Na, and Pa that were also evoked by unaltered speech.
source: Figure 2A shows that overall there were morphological similarities between responses to both types of speech; however, there were more early and late component waves to broadband peaky speech. More specifically, whereas both types of speech evoked waves V, Na, and Pa, broadband peaky speech also evoked waves I, often III (14–19 of 22 subjects depending on whether a 30 or 150 Hz high-pass filter cutoff was used), and P0.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and described in the text.

claim: Wave V was more robust and sharper to broadband peaky speech but peaked slightly later than the broader wave V to unaltered speech.
source: Wave V was more robust and sharper to broadband peaky speech but peaked slightly later than the broader wave V to unaltered speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of waveforms in the study.

claim: Mean peak latencies for waves V, Na, and Pa were longer for broadband peaky than unaltered speech by 0.87 ± 0.06 ms, 6.92 ± 0.44 ms, and 1.07 ± 0.45 ms, respectively.
source: As suggested by the waveforms in Figure 2A, mean ± SEM peak latencies for waves V, Na, and Pa were longer for broadband peaky than unaltered speech by 0.87 ± 0.06 ms (independent t-test, t(21) = 14.7, p<0.01, d = 3.22), 6.92 ± 0.44 ms (t(21) = 15.4, p<0.01, d = 3.44), and 1.07 ± 0.45 ms (t(20) = 2.3, p=0.032, d = 0.52), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: The pre-stimulus component in broadband peaky speech responses was present in both linear and auditory nerve models.
source: The pre-stimulus component of the measured response was present in both models, suggesting that there are nonlinear parts of the response that are not accounted for in the deconvolution with the pulse train regressor.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The pre-stimulus component suggests there are nonlinear parts of the response not accounted for in the deconvolution with the pulse train regressor.
source: The pre-stimulus component of the measured response was present in both models, suggesting that there are nonlinear parts of the response that are not accounted for in the deconvolution with the pulse train regressor.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from simulation results.

claim: The pre-stimulus component was reduced with a 150-Hz first-order Butterworth high-pass filter and minimized with a 200-Hz second-order Butterworth high-pass filter.
source: The pre-stimulus component was reduced with a 150-Hz first-order Butterworth high-pass filter (Figure 1) and minimized with a more aggressive 200-Hz second-order Butterworth high-pass filter (Figure 3, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: EEG data collected in response to broadband peaky speech can be regressed with half-wave rectified speech to generate a response similar to that from unaltered speech.
source: Figure 4A shows that the derived responses to unaltered and broadband peaky speech were similar in morphology when using the half-wave rectified audio as the regressor. Correlation coefficients from the 22 subjects for the 0–40 ms lags had a median (interquartile range) of 0.84 (0.72–0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and correlation coefficients.

claim: Regressing EEG from unaltered speech with the pulse train does not give a robust canonical response.
source: Figure 4B shows that simply using the pulse train as a regressor does not give a robust canonical response – the response contained a wave that slightly resembled wave V of the response to broadband peaky speech, albeit at a later latency and smaller amplitude, but there were no other earlier waves of the ABR or later waves of the MLR.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The group average waveforms to female- and male-narrated broadband peaky speech showed similar canonical morphologies but were smaller and later for female-narrated ABR responses.
source: The group average waveforms to female- and male-narrated broadband peaky speech showed similar canonical morphologies but were smaller and later for female-narrated ABR responses (Figure 5A), much as they would be for click stimuli presented at higher rates (e.g., Burkard et al., 1990; Burkard and Hecox, 1983; Chiappa et al., 1979; Don et al., 1977; Jiang et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and comparison to cited literature.

claim: Fewer subjects exhibited a clear wave III in the female-narrated response (9 versus all 11 subjects).
source: All component waves of the ABR and MLR were visible in the group average, although fewer subjects exhibited a clear wave III in the female-narrated response (9 versus all 11 subjects).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Mean peak latency differences (female – male) for waves I, III, and V of the ABR were 0.21 ± 0.13 ms, 0.42 ± 0.11 ms, and 0.54 ± 0.09 ms, respectively.
source: Mean ± SEM peak latency differences (female – male) for waves I, III, and V of the ABR were 0.21 ± 0.13 ms (t(10) = 1.59, p=0.144, d = 0.50), 0.42 ± 0.11 ms (t(9) = 3.47, p=0.007, d = 1.16), and 0.54 ± 0.09 ms (t(10) = 5.56, p<0.001, d = 1.76), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: Frequency-specific responses to multiband peaky speech showed characteristic ABR and MLR waves with longer latencies for lower frequency bands.
source: Overall, the frequency-specific responses showed characteristic ABR and MLR waves with longer latencies for lower frequency bands, as would be expected from responses arising from different cochlear regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and comparison to expected cochlear physiology.

claim: Waves I and III of the ABR were visible in the group average waveforms of the 2–4 kHz (≥41% of subjects) and 4–8 kHz (≥86% of subjects) bands.
source: Also, waves I and III of the ABR were visible in the group average waveforms of the 2–4 kHz (≥41% of subjects) and 4–8 kHz (≥86% of subjects) bands, whereas the MLR waves were more prominent in the 0–1 kHz (≥95% of subjects) and 1–2 kHz (≥54% of subjects) bands.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: MLR waves were more prominent in the 0–1 kHz (≥95% of subjects) and 1–2 kHz (≥54% of subjects) bands.
source: Also, waves I and III of the ABR were visible in the group average waveforms of the 2–4 kHz (≥41% of subjects) and 4–8 kHz (≥86% of subjects) bands, whereas the MLR waves were more prominent in the 0–1 kHz (≥95% of subjects) and 1–2 kHz (≥54% of subjects) bands.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: There was a significant decrease in wave V latency with increasing frequency band.
source: There was a significant decrease in wave V latency with increasing frequency band (slope p<0.001 for 30 and 150 Hz), which was shallower (i.e., less negative) for MLR waves compared to the ABR wave V (all p<0.001 for interactions between wave and frequency term).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from the study.

claim: The summed multiband response was strikingly similar in morphology to the broadband peaky speech response.
source: As shown in Figure 7, this summed multiband response was strikingly similar in morphology to the broadband peaky speech. Both responses were high-passed filtered at 150 Hz and 30 Hz to highlight the earlier ABR waves and later MLR waves, respectively. The median (interquartile range) correlation coefficients from the 22 subjects were 0.90 (0.84–0.94) for 0–15 ms ABR lags and 0.66 (0.55–0.83) for 0–40 ms MLR lags.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 and correlation coefficients.

claim: Responses to both male and female narrators showed similar morphology, but the responses were smaller and the MLR waves more variable for the female than the male narrator.
source: As with broadband peaky speech, responses to both narrators showed similar morphology, but the responses were smaller and the MLR waves more variable for the female than the male narrator (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Median male–female correlation coefficients for multiband responses ranged from 0.12 (−0.11–0.34) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.44 (0.32–0.49) for the 4–8 kHz band for MLR lags.
source: The median (interquartile range) male–female correlation coefficients were better for higher frequency bands, ranging from 0.12 (−0.11–0.34) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.44 (0.32–0.49) for the 4–8 kHz band for MLR lags (Figure 8B, left), and from 0.49 (0.30–0.69) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.79 (0.64–0.81) for the 4–8 kHz band for ABR lags (Figure 8B, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Median male–female correlation coefficients for multiband responses ranged from 0.49 (0.30–0.69) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.79 (0.64–0.81) for the 4–8 kHz band for ABR lags.
source: The median (interquartile range) male–female correlation coefficients were better for higher frequency bands, ranging from 0.12 (−0.11–0.34) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.44 (0.32–0.49) for the 4–8 kHz band for MLR lags (Figure 8B, left), and from 0.49 (0.30–0.69) for the 1–2 kHz band to 0.79 (0.64–0.81) for the 4–8 kHz band for ABR lags (Figure 8B, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Waves I and III of the ABR were visible in the group average waveforms of the 4 kHz band (≥45% and 18% of subjects for the male and female narrator, respectively) and 8 kHz band (≥90% and 72% of subjects for the male and female narrator, respectively) for dichotic multiband speech.
source: Also, waves I and III of the ABR were visible in the group average waveforms of the 4 kHz band (≥45% and 18% of subjects for the male and female narrator, respectively) and 8 kHz band (≥90% and 72% of subjects for the male and female narrator, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Median left–right ear correlation coefficients for dichotic multiband speech ranged from 0.28 (0.02–0.52) for the 0.5 kHz band to 0.73 (0.62–0.84) for the 8 kHz band.
source: As shown in Figure 9B, the median (interquartile range) left–right ear correlation coefficients (averaged across narrators) ranged from 0.28 (0.02–0.52) for the 0.5 kHz band to 0.73 (0.62–0.84) for the 8 kHz band.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Male–female correlation coefficients for dichotic multiband speech ranged from 0.44 (0.00–0.58) for the 0.5 kHz band to 0.76 (0.51–0.80) for the 8 kHz band.
source: Male–female correlation coefficients (averaged across ear) ranged from 0.44 (0.00–0.58) for the 0.5 kHz band to 0.76 (0.51–0.80) for the 8 kHz band.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: Acquisition times for 22 subjects were similar for responses to both unaltered and broadband peaky male-narrated speech, with 0 dB SNR achieved by 7–8 min in 50% of subjects and about 20 min for all subjects.
source: Acquisition times for 22 subjects were similar for responses to both unaltered and broadband peaky male-narrated speech, with 0 dB SNR achieved by 7–8 min in 50% of subjects and about 20 min for all subjects.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 10.

claim: For responses high-pass filtered at 150 Hz to highlight the ABR, the time to reach 0 dB SNR reduced to 2 and 5 min for 50% and 100% of subjects respectively for broadband peaky speech.
source: For responses high-pass filtered at 150 Hz to highlight the ABR (0–15 ms interval), the time reduced to 2 and 5 min for 50% and 100% of subjects respectively for broadband peaky speech but increased to 8 and >20 min for 50% and 100% of subjects respectively for unaltered speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 10.

claim: Acquisition times were at least 2.1 times – but in some cases over 10 times – longer for female-narrated broadband peaky speech compared to male-narrated speech.
source: However, acquisition times were at least 2.1 times – but in some cases over 10 times – longer for female-narrated broadband peaky speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 10.

claim: 72% of subjects had frequency-specific responses with ≥0 dB SNR for all four frequency bands by the end of the 32 min recording for male-narrated multiband speech.
source: Many subjects (72%) had frequency-specific responses (common component subtracted) with ≥0 dB SNR for all four frequency bands by the end of the 32 min recording for the male-narrated speech, but this was achieved in only 45% of subjects for the female-narrated speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 11A.

claim: 45% of subjects had frequency-specific responses with ≥0 dB SNR for all four frequency bands by the end of the 32 min recording for female-narrated multiband speech.
source: Many subjects (72%) had frequency-specific responses (common component subtracted) with ≥0 dB SNR for all four frequency bands by the end of the 32 min recording for the male-narrated speech, but this was achieved in only 45% of subjects for the female-narrated speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 11A.

claim: 50% of subjects achieved 0 dB SNR by 15 min for male-narrated multiband responses across the ABR 0–15 ms interval.
source: Multiband peaky speech required significantly longer recording times than broadband peaky speech, with 50% of subjects achieving 0 dB SNR by 15 min compared to 2 min for the male-narrated responses across the ABR 0–15 ms interval and 17 min compared to 5 min for the MLR 0–30 ms interval.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 11A.

claim: All 10 audiological band responses achieved ≥ 0 dB SNR in 45% of ears by 64 min for male-narrated dichotic speech.
source: All 10 audiological band responses achieved ≥ 0 dB SNR in 45% of ears (10/22 ears from 11 subjects) by 64 min for male-narrated speech and in 27% of ears (6/22 ears) for female-narrated speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 11B.

claim: All 10 audiological band responses achieved ≥ 0 dB SNR in 27% of ears for female-narrated dichotic speech.
source: All 10 audiological band responses achieved ≥ 0 dB SNR in 45% of ears (10/22 ears from 11 subjects) by 64 min for male-narrated speech and in 27% of ears (6/22 ears) for female-narrated speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The average fundamental frequency was 115 Hz for the male narrator and 198 Hz for the female narrator.
source: The average fundamental frequency was 115 Hz for the male narrator and 198 Hz for the female narrator.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the audiobook stimuli.

claim: 38 unique subjects (25 females, 66%) were aged 18–32 years with a mean ± SD age of 23.0 ± 3.6 years.
source: The 38 unique subjects (25 females, 66%) were aged 18–32 years with a mean ± SD age of 23.0 ± 3.6 years.
evidence: The claim describes the participant demographics.

claim: All subjects had normal hearing in both ears, defined as thresholds ≤20 dB HL from 250 to 8000 Hz.
source: Audiometric screening confirmed subjects had normal hearing in both ears, defined as thresholds ≤20 dB HL from 250 to 8000 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the hearing status of participants.

claim: Speech was presented at an average level of 65 dB SPL over ER-2 insert earphones.
source: Speech was presented at an average level of 65 dB SPL over ER-2 insert earphones (Etymotic Research, Elk Grove, IL) plugged into an RME Babyface Pro digital sound card (RME, Haimhausen, Germany) via an HB7 headphone amplifier (Tucker Davis Technologies, Alachua, FL).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: EEG was sampled at 10,000 Hz and high-pass filtered at 0.1 Hz during recording.
source: Data were sampled at 10,000 Hz and high-pass filtered at 0.1 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the EEG recording parameters.

claim: The intraclass correlation coefficient type 3 for all peaks were ≥0.90, indicating excellent reliability for the chosen peak latencies.
source: The intraclass correlation coefficient type 3 (absolute agreement) was used to verify good agreement in peak latencies chosen by an experienced audiologist and neuroscientist (MJP) at two different time points, 3 months apart. The ICC3 for all peaks were ≥0.90, indicating excellent reliability for the chosen peak latencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by reliability analysis of the data.
